answer.label: Not Ayn Rand — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: 1905–1982 · Russian-American novelist & philosopher (the idea only, not the wording)
answer.sourceLine: Rand never wrote this sentence. Quote Investigator ↗ thinks it was probably made by merging two lines of dialogue in The Fountainhead (1943). In that scene the Dean asks Howard Roark “My dear fellow, who will let you?” and Roark answers “That’s not the point. The point is, who will stop me?” The Ayn Rand Institute ↗ agrees that the source lies in that passage.

source.heading: The real lines: a dialogue in The Fountainhead

docMeta.dd: The Dean of the Stanton Institute of Technology, and Howard Roark (Chapter I)

source.excerpt:
“Do you mean to tell me that you’re thinking seriously of building that way, when and if you are an architect?”
“Yes.”
“My dear fellow, who will let you?”
“That’s not the point. The point is, who will stop me?”
source.trailTitle: How a two-line dialogue became a one-line slogan
trail: 1943: In the opening chapter of The Fountainhead, the Dean asks Roark “My dear fellow, who will let you?” and Roark replies “That’s not the point. The point is, who will stop me?” (Wikiquote, sourced ↗)

2001: Janet Lowe’s Welch: An American Icon uses a one-line version as a chapter epigraph, credited “Ayn Rand, The Fountainhead.” Quote Investigator notes that this sentence is not in the novel (Quote Investigator ↗)

2013: Forbes’s “Top 100 Inspirational Quotes” lists the exact wording at number 93, credited to Rand. That October, Time reports on a Forever 21 shirt printed with it, and Quote Investigator then publishes its investigation (Quote Investigator ↗)
2019–2021: PolitiFact rates the attribution Mostly False (PolitiFact ↗). The Ayn Rand Institute writes that Rand “never wrote or said the exact words attributed to her” (New Ideal ↗)
source.excerptNote: The Dean speaks first and Roark replies. This is Quote Investigator’s transcription from a Signet reprint of the 1943 Bobbs-Merrill edition. The popular sentence, “The question isn’t who is going to let me; it’s who is going to stop me,” does not appear in the novel.

source.rightsNote: The popular one-liner is an anonymous paraphrase and has no identifiable source of its own. The dialogue shown here comes from The Fountainhead, first published in 1943, which is after the 1931 public-domain cutoff. It is therefore treated as in copyright in the United States, held by Rand’s estate and/or publisher, and is quoted here only briefly, for commentary.

author.name: Ayn Rand
author.heading: About Ayn Rand
author.bio: Ayn Rand was born Alisa Zinovyevna Rosenbaum in Saint Petersburg in 1905 and died in New York City in 1982. She was a Russian-American writer and philosopher who named her philosophical system Objectivism. She is best known for the novels We the Living (1936), The Fountainhead (1943) and Atlas Shrugged (1957). The sentiment behind this quote belongs to Howard Roark, the hero of The Fountainhead, but the popular one-sentence wording does not appear in her work.

misattribution.heading: How the line got pinned on Rand
misattribution.intro: The sentence circulates as if Rand wrote it, sometimes even with a book credit. Quote Investigator could not find it in any of her writings and thinks it is a later merger of two lines of dialogue spoken by different characters.

items.why: The Ayn Rand Institute says Rand “never wrote or said the exact words attributed to her,” while agreeing that their source lies in a Fountainhead passage (New Ideal ↗).

Janet Lowe’s Welch: An American Icon credited the sentence to the novel. Quote Investigator says the sentence is not in the named novel and that even the quoted phrases are off: the novel says “who will let you” and “who will stop me” (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.scope: Forbes list and a Forever 21 shirt, 2013
items.why: Forbes listed the exact wording at number 93 of its “Top 100 Inspirational Quotes,” and a Forever 21 “Unstoppable Muscle Tee” printed it with Rand’s name. Both are documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
PolitiFact rated the attribution Mostly False. It found that the quote paraphrases an exchange between the Dean and Howard Roark (PolitiFact ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The real source is a two-speaker exchange in The Fountainhead (1943). The Dean asks “My dear fellow, who will let you?” and Howard Roark answers “That’s not the point. The point is, who will stop me?” (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the original wording matters
lead: In the novel the line belongs to a scene, not a slogan. Howard Roark has been expelled from the Stanton Institute of Technology for refusing to design in borrowed historical styles. The Dean asks whether he really means to build that way and who would let him, and Roark turns the question around: the point is who will stop him.

Ben Bayer, a fellow at the Ayn Rand Institute, told PolitiFact ↗: “This is an attribution to Rand that has really spread all over the internet.” He also warned that, out of context, the rewritten line can suggest anyone should be able to do anything they like, which he said is not Rand’s view.
detailsBody: According to Quote Investigator ↗, the 2003 workplace book Love It, Don’t Leave It: 26 Ways to Get What You Want at Work printed the sentence with no attribution at all, and treated it critically as the attitude of someone who should learn to yield occasionally.
context.pull: “That’s not the point. The point is, who will stop me?”
